subject: Cognitive Science
title: Broadbent's Filter Theory
description: Learn Broadbent's Filter Theory in one minute.

hook.text: In World War II, air traffic controllers had to track multiple radio channels at once—and failed.

buildup.text: Donald Broadbent studied this and proposed the first model: an early selection filter.

discovery.text: His filter sits before meaning extraction. Unattended messages are blocked at the physical level.

twist.text: But the cocktail party effect broke his model—your name gets through even when filtered out.

climax.text: Broadbent's filter was too strict, but he launched the modern science of selective attention.

punchline.text: The first filter theory was wrong—but beautifully so.

quiz.question: Where did Broadbent place the attention filter?

details.summary: Donald Broadbent proposed that attention works like an early filter, blocking unattended information before it reaches conscious awareness. Based on dichotic listening experiments, his 1958 model was the first systematic theory of selective attention and launched decades of research.
details.whyItMatters: Broadbent's filter theory was the foundation of modern attention research. Its limitations sparked rival theories that deepened our understanding of how the brain selects information.
takeaways: Broadbent proposed an early selection filter for attention
Unattended information was thought to be blocked completely
The theory was based on dichotic listening experiments

faq.question: What is a dichotic listening experiment?
faq.answer: Participants wear headphones and hear different messages in each ear simultaneously. They shadow or repeat one message aloud while ignoring the other. Researchers then test how much of the ignored message was processed to reveal filtering mechanisms.

faq.question: Why was Broadbent's filter theory eventually challenged?
faq.answer: Evidence like the cocktail party effect showed that meaningful unattended information, such as your own name, could break through the filter. This suggested that some processing of unattended input occurs before filtering, contradicting strict early selection.
